definitions.definition: First stage of knowledge: the wish, preceded by dispassion, to leave foolishness and turn to scripture and the good.
Second stage: taking up right conduct through contact with scripture and the good, with dispassion and practice.
Third stage: non-attachment to sense-objects arising from the first two, desire having become thin.
Fourth stage: the mind, from practice of the first three, rests in pure sattva (the state of the Self).
Fifth stage: from practice of the four, non-association with objects becomes firm and the wonder of sattva is established.
Sixth stage: delighting in the Self, one no longer conceives inner or outer objects and understands them only when long prompted by others.
Seventh stage: with no difference perceived, abiding solely in one's own nature; the turya state of those liberated while living.

equivalents.note: the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha itself calls the seventh stage the turya state of the jīvanmukta (3.118.16); turyagā names the stage, turīya the state

literal: the one gone to the fourth

definitions.definition: A stage (ground) of knowledge; the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha counts seven, with liberation beyond them, and says others count the stages of yoga differently.
The state beyond the fourth, the domain of those liberated without a body (videhamukta), lying beyond the seventh stage.
A stage of ignorance; seven are taught: seed-waking, waking, great waking, waking-dream, dream, dream-waking and deep sleep, each branching a hundredfold.
Seed-waking: the first pure, nameless stirring of consciousness, the seed of the future names 'jīva' and the like.
Great waking: the notion 'this is I, this is mine' grown firm through past births.
Waking-dream: the waking mind's fancies and misperceptions (two moons, silver in shell, mirage).
Dream-waking: a dream taken as waking and grown into great waking, as in a dream-body sustained for long.
The four gatekeepers at the door of liberation: peace (śama), inquiry (vicāra), contentment (santoṣa) and holy company (sādhusaṅgama); mastering one brings the others.

literal: gatekeeper of the door of liberation

definitions.definition: Peace or calm, the first gatekeeper: the cooling of the desert of saṃsāra, called the supreme state and the end of delusion.
The intellect fixed on the Lord (Uddhava Gītā's redefinition).
Inquiry: discriminating reflection, guided by scripture and the wise, into what one is and what the world is; the second gatekeeper and the lamp by which the real is seen.
Contentment: not craving the unobtained and enjoying what comes without elation or dejection; the third gatekeeper.
Contentment (tuṣṭi), one of the Uddhava Gītā's twelve niyamas.
Company of the holy (sādhusaṅgama), the fourth gatekeeper, from which discrimination arises.
Association with the holy, which wins the Lord more than yoga, Sāṃkhya or austerity; attachment itself, directed to the holy, becomes the open door to liberation.
The first of the nine means of devotion taught to Śabarī.

Human effort: mental and bodily activity guided by the instruction of the good and by scripture; by it everything is attained. It is twofold, former (whose fruit is called fate) and present, and the present overcomes the former.

equivalents.note: puruṣakāra, the usual epic/smṛti word for human effort opposed to daiva

definitions.definition: Fate: in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha nothing but one's own former effort (prāk-pauruṣa); a name given to the fruit of one's deeds, without form, act or power of its own; relying on it is delusion.
The 'crow and palm-fruit' coincidence: used for the uncaused, chance-like arising of the world-appearance and of the turn toward inquiry.

literal: like the crow and the palm fruit

definitions.definition: Latent tendency: the grasping of an object through firm conception without reflection; one of the two seeds of mind; impure vāsanās bind to rebirth, pure ones (friendliness and the like) are to be cultivated before all are given up; bondage is bondage to vāsanā.
Exhaustion of latent tendencies; the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha equates it with liberation ('mokṣaḥ syād vāsanākṣayaḥ').
Destruction of the mind: not the loss of function but the end of the shrinking notions 'this is I, this is not I'; the state of the one liberated while living, in which pure sattva arises.
The vibration of the life-breath, one of the two seeds of the mind: when it moves awareness arises, when it rests the mind does not arise.

equivalents.note: shares the word spanda with Kashmir Śaivism, where spanda is the divine self-vibration of consciousness; in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha passage it is the breath's movement; not asserted as the same

definitions.definition: Firm conception or imagining, the second seed of the mind, identified with vāsanā.
The space of consciousness: the knower within and without all beings that reveals existence; mind-space and elemental space arise from it.
The space of mind: the creator pervading all through its conceiving.
Elemental space, extended in the ten directions, the support of wind and clouds.
The seen, the whole world of objects; the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha's teaching turns on the realization that the seen does not exist apart from consciousness.
Wiping away of the seen: the mind's erasure of the world through the knowledge 'the seen does not exist', from which the bliss of nirvāṇa arises.
Practice of Brahman: thinking of it, speaking of it, awakening one another to it and being wholly devoted to it.
The 'kingdom of the mind': fancy or day-dream, which in the stories (Śukra, Lavaṇa) creates whole lives.
Conceiving or willing by the mind, by which worlds are spun; its cessation is the end of saṃsāra.
The 'great doer' who does whatever comes, without regard to attraction, aversion, merit and demerit, free of ego, like a witness.
The 'great enjoyer' who hates nothing, praises nothing and enjoys all that comes.
The 'great renouncer' who has given up all notions of dharma and adharma, desire and thought.
Liberation while living: in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha the seventh stage, in which one acts as custom requires, unimmersed in pleasure and pain, the mind 'dead' (manonāśa).
The liberated one, though in the body, is not in it; his functions are free of intention; the body lives on while its karma lasts.
The destruction of ignorance, the fruit of human birth and the state of liberation while living.
Bodiless liberation, the domain beyond the fourth (turyātīta).
One who has 'shaken off' all worldly ties, a liberated wanderer who behaves like a child, madman or dullard; the teacher of King Yadu.

Defined syllable by syllable: a — free of the noose of hope, ever in bliss; va — free of vāsanās, living in the present; dhū — dust-grey limbs, cleansed mind, free of concentration and meditation; ta — held to truth, free of anxiety, darkness and ego.

Teacher: the self is its own chief teacher; yet ignorance-bound persons need a knower of the principles to give knowledge; the avadhūta takes twenty-four teachers from nature; the guru is the helmsman of the human boat.
In the Guru Gītā: 'gu' is darkness, 'ru' its remover; the guru is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara and the supreme Brahman; the root of liberation is his grace.
The guru-principle, without knowing which sacrifice, vows and pilgrimage are fruitless; the guru as not other than the Self.
The bee's way of begging: taking a little food from many houses without troubling any.
The python's way of living: accepting whatever food comes unsought, lying still if none comes.
Freedom from hope or expectation, called the highest happiness by Piṅgalā.
Disgust or disenchantment with worldly aims, the sword that cuts the noose of hope; for the Bhikṣu a raft sent by the Lord.
Devotion: the natural, motiveless inclination of the senses and mind toward the Lord, greater than liberation; by it alone the Lord is attained; it purifies even outcastes.
Loving devotion to Rāma, the lamp without which knowledge does not shine and the cause of liberation; open to men, women and even animals.
Devotion to the Goddess, the easiest of the three paths, graded by the guṇas and culminating in supreme devotion.
Devotion without motive and without interruption to the Supreme Person, flowing to him like the Gaṅgā to the sea (Kapila); also 'animittā'.

equivalents.note: both name the highest, desireless devotion beyond the guṇa-graded forms; the Kapila Gītā's devotee refuses oneness, whereas the Devī Gītā's supreme devotion ends in non-dual knowledge

definitions.definition: Attributeless devotion: the fourth, highest devotion beyond the tāmasa, rājasa and sāttvika forms, by which one transcends the guṇas.
Supreme devotion to the Goddess beyond the guṇa-graded forms, seeing her in all beings and ending in non-dual knowledge.
The yoga of devotion, fitting one in whom faith in the Lord's stories has arisen, who is neither disgusted with nor too attached to the world.
The yoga of knowledge, fitting those disgusted with action who have renounced it.
The yoga of action, fitting those not yet disgusted who still have desires; performed without desire, it purifies and leads to knowledge or devotion.
In the Uddhava Gītā: ritual worship of the Lord — Vedic, tantric or mixed — in an image, ground, fire, sun, water or the heart.

notes: Distinct from the Yoga Sūtra's kriyā-yoga (austerity, study, devotion to Īśvara).

definitions.definition: Yogic power: eighteen are listed (eight chief, ten from the guṇas) plus lesser ones; they are obstacles and a waste of time for one seeking the Lord.
The fourth, the Lord in whom one abides beyond the intellect's states of waking, dream and sleep, of which the jīva is the witness.
The witness distinct from the three states of the intellect (Haṃsa Gītā); the non-eating bird that knows both.
The Self as witness of the elements, body and mind, free and actionless; resting in it is freedom now (Aṣṭāvakra); the Self standing apart as the intellect's witness (Rāma Gītā).

The three qualities belong to the intellect, not to the self; everything is classed by them with a fourth, attributeless class belonging to the Lord; one conquers rajas and tamas by sattva and sattva by desirelessness.
Possession or grasping, which brings suffering in proportion to how dear the thing is (the osprey).
Indirect or veiled statement: the Vedic seers speak indirectly and the indirect is dear to the Lord.
The mind, declared the supreme cause that turns the wheel of saṃsāra (Bhikṣu Gītā); attached to the guṇas it binds, devoted to the Person it frees (Kapila).
Time, counted by Kapila as the twenty-fifth principle and identified with the Lord, from whom prakṛti's movement arises.
From the unmanifest arose time, pradhāna and the supreme person (Īśvara Gītā).
The unmanifest pradhāna of three guṇas, cause and effect in one; in Kapila's teaching it is powerless before the self that sees with knowledge, dispassion and devotion.
The person, beginningless, beyond prakṛti, not touched by its qualities, like the sun reflected in water.
Liberation as residence in the Lord's world; one of the five that pure devotees refuse without service.
Liberation as equal lordly power with the Lord.
Liberation as nearness to the Lord.
Liberation as having a form like the Lord's.
Oneness with the Lord (merging), the fifth kind of liberation, which pure devotees do not accept.

equivalents.note: later Vaiṣṇava lists name the fifth liberation sāyujya; the Bhāgavata verse says ekatva

definitions.definition: One's own glory, in which the realized abides and for which the categories of dharma, duality, time, states and samādhi no longer apply.
Abiding in oneself, not attained by study of scriptures without 'forgetting everything'.

In the Aṣṭāvakra Gītā, 'dissolution' of the world into the Self by four recognitions (space and pot, ocean and waves, shell and silver, all in me), after which there is nothing to renounce, accept or dissolve.

notes: Distinct from laya-yoga of the haṭha texts.

definitions.definition: The inclination toward non-duality, which arises only by the grace of the Lord.
Primal nature, identified with Sītā, who creates, preserves and dissolves by Rāma's mere presence and performs the deeds superimposed on him.
The unmanifest root nature as the Lord's power resting in him (Īśvara Gītā 2.7.30).
The reflection of consciousness in the intellect, compared to the sky reflected in a pond; unreal, a product of ignorance; the jīva as agent (Rāma-hṛdaya, Rāma Gītā).
Delimitation: consciousness delimited by the intellect, like the space enclosed by a pond; its identity with the whole is taught by the great sayings.
The Goddess appears divided by adjuncts like the space in pots.
The great saying ('that thou art' and the like) that teaches the identity of the delimited consciousness with the whole; understood by partial implication.
Partial implication: the mode by which 'that' and 'thou' are understood as their common consciousness, dropping the opposed features, as in 'this is that Devadatta'.

equivalents.note: the Rāma Gītā names it bhāga-lakṣaṇā after rejecting jahatī and ajahatī; later Advaita manuals call the same jahad-ajahal-lakṣaṇā

definitions.definition: The projecting power of māyā that creates the gross and subtle world.
The veiling power of māyā that covers knowledge.

Superimposition: the appearance of one thing as another through error, like a snake in a rope; ego is the first superimposition on the Self; jīva and witness appear mutually superimposed like fire and iron.
The notion of self in the non-self by which saṃsāra is imagined; it has the powers of projection and veiling.
The Goddess's own inseparable power, neither real nor unreal nor both; conventionally called ignorance, in truth not other than her.
The power by which all that is grasped by mind and senses is a perishable mental creation; bondage and liberation are said by reference to its guṇas.

The nine means of devotion taught to Śabarī: holy company, talk of Rāma's stories, singing his qualities, expounding his words, guileless service of the teacher as Rāma, virtuous conduct with steady worship, worship through his mantra, honouring devotees and seeing him in all with dispassion, and inquiry into his nature.

notes: The Bhāgavata's nine forms (7.5.23: hearing, singing, remembering ...) are a different list.

definitions.definition: The coiled power in the root centre, meditated upon at dawn as moving up and down the inner path and led through the six centres to union with the supreme.
The Goddess's seed-syllable hrīṃ ('heart-letter'), placed in the body in daily worship.
The Goddess's cosmic form, shown to the gods and worshipped in Vedic worship.
The union of the jīva and the Self (Devī Gītā).
Not union with wealth, kin, powers, heavens or divine ranks, but the undivided understanding regarding Śiva, Viṣṇu, Śakti, the Sun and Gaṇeśa (Gaṇeśa Gītā).
One-pointedness of mind on the Lord by stopping other modifications, with eight means (Īśvara Gītā).

The yoga of smearing the body with sacred ash while reciting the 'agnir iti' mantras and meditating on Īśāna as the supreme light, for freeing the bound soul; called the essence of Vedānta and 'beyond the stages of life'.
Beyond the stages of life: the Pāśupata observance so described by revelation.
Sacred ash from the sacred fire, smeared on all the limbs in the Pāśupata yoga.
Ash used in the Virajā initiation (Śiva Gītā).
All selves wandering in saṃsāra, the Lord's 'cattle'.
The noose of māyā with which the Lord binds the paśus in play.
Śiva as Paśupati, lord of the bound selves, who binds them and alone frees them.
The 'Virajā' initiation of the Śiva Gītā, in which the body is smeared with ash while reciting the Virajā mantras, taking the Pāśupata vow.
